beats.narration_text: Hej — this is Liam, in for Komal. A logo used to be the mark you could see from across the room. Now houses put a file in the bag: where it was made, what it is made of. Today: whether knowing that is the new luxury mark, what a passport actually is, and one capsule already carrying a digital product passport you can tap.

beats.narration_text: Start with names. A logo is a public mark of rank — other people can see it. Authenticity answers: is this the real object. Provenance answers: where, how, and who made it. Those are not synonyms.

beats.narration_text: Why this is live now. In April twenty twenty-one, L.V.M.H., Prada, and Cartier founded Aura — a consortium chain for product history and authenticity. Europe is writing a legal product passport. Batteries must carry one from February twenty twenty-seven. For textiles, the delegated act is planned for late twenty twenty-seven — not mandatory on fashion yet.

beats.narration_text: What it changed. Consortium: Aura records authenticity, ownership, and a claimed lifecycle. Law: a Digital Product Passport is a product identity the market has to carry. Score: Fashion Revolution still asks whether they published who made the clothes. A certificate is not a factory list.

beats.narration_text: Worked example. Prada Re-Nylon for Sea Beyond. Each piece carries an N.F.C. tag. Tap it, and Aura opens a digital product passport: origin, components, water, energy, carbon. From March twenty twenty-six, a selection can claim a Certificate of Ownership. Brand-controlled. Not the E.U. textile act. Not a logo.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A logo is a public signal. Authenticity is a certificate. Provenance is a file. Aura is the industry rail. Europe is writing the legal one — batteries first, textiles later. Design judgment: if other people cannot see it, it is not a logo. Ask what the file actually contains, and who can read it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude with a product you actually own or sell — a bag, a jacket, a watch. (1) Logo, certificate, or provenance file — which machine is in front of you? (2) What would a false origin cost in that field? (3) Who can read the file: you, a reseller, a regulator, a stranger across the room? Score it: public mark, or private audit. Run it before the next transparency meeting.
